Standard accessors for a fitted mysterymodel

Source: R/accessors.R
mm_model-accessors.Rd

mm_model() stores the fitted rms object at model$fit, and until these methods existed a caller had to reach into it to get a coefficient. Each method below delegates where delegation gives the right statistical semantics and does the work explicitly where it does not.

Three of them could not delegate, which is why they are written out rather than aliased. Each case was established by running the generic against a fitted lrm object, not inferred from the object's shape:

  • stats::fitted() on an rms::lrm() fit returns NULL, because lrm() does not populate fitted.values. A delegating method would hand back NULL and look like it worked.

  • stats::confint() on such a fit fails: it dispatches to confint.glm(), begins profiling, and errors with $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors. There is therefore no profile-likelihood interval to preserve, and the Wald interval here is a documented substitute rather than a silent one.

  • stats::summary() on an rms fit reports effect sizes across the predictor ranges, which is a different object from a model summary. A delegating summary.mm_model() would return something a reader would misread, so this one composes its own and names where the other lives.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
coef(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
vcov(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
formula(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
nobs(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
fitted(object, scale = c("response", "link"), ...)

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
residuals(object, type = "deviance", ...)

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
confint(object, parm, level = 0.95, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mm_model'
summary(object, level = 0.95, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary.mm_model'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

object, x

A mm_model from mm_model().

...

Passed to the underlying rms method where one is used.

scale

"response" for probabilities, "link" for the linear predictor.

type

Residual type, passed to rms.

parm

Coefficients to report; defaults to all.

level

Coverage.

Value

As documented per method below.

Functions

  • coef(mm_model): Model coefficients, names preserved.

  • vcov(mm_model): The coefficient variance-covariance matrix.

  • formula(mm_model): The fitted formula. Its response term is the package's internal recoded outcome (.mm_y), not the column named in mm_project(outcome = ); object$project$outcome is that column.

  • nobs(mm_model): The number of observations the model was fitted on, which is the development rows after complete-case exclusion, not the rows supplied. object$n_supplied and object$n_held are the other two counts, and they are different numbers on purpose.

  • fitted(mm_model): Fitted values. scale = "response" (the default) gives predicted probabilities; scale = "link" gives the linear predictor. The scale is an argument rather than an assumption because rms::lrm() leaves fitted.values empty, so there is no inherited convention to follow.

  • residuals(mm_model): Residuals. type is passed to rms::residuals.lrm(), which supports "ordinary", "li.shepherd", "score", "pearson", "deviance", "pseudo.dep", "partial", "dfbeta" and "gof". The default is "deviance". "score", "partial" and "dfbeta" return a matrix rather than a vector, and the types are not interchangeable: a residual's interpretation follows its definition, so read ?rms::residuals.lrm before comparing two of them.

  • confint(mm_model): Wald confidence intervals on the coefficients, from vcov().

    These are Wald intervals, and that is a substitute rather than a preference. stats::confint() on an rms::lrm() fit dispatches to confint.glm(), which attempts profile likelihood and errors, so no profile interval is available to return. They are intervals on the coefficient scale and are not the interval mm_validate() reports on the c-statistic, which is a DeLong interval on a performance measure. Reading one as the other misreports the model.

  • summary(mm_model): A summary of the fitted model: its call, the three row counts, the parameter budget, and the coefficients with their Wald intervals.

    It reports no performance. Discrimination, calibration and bootstrap optimism come from mm_validate(), and a fitted-model summary that printed them beside the coefficients would invite a reader to treat an apparent number as a validated one. rms::summary() on object$fit is a different object again: effect sizes across predictor ranges.

  • print(summary.mm_model): Print method for the summary.

See also

mm_validate() for performance, which these do not report.
